timecoded_text_to_speech.text: I'm Matthew Miller, I work for Red Hat and I am the Fedora Project Leader.
My name is Jonathan Deeter, I am a system administrator for a school in Beirut, Lebanon.
My name is Shimonthro, I work for Red Hat for Fedora QA team and I am a quality engineer.
My name is Mike DiPolo, I contribute to Fedora in my free time.
I'm a packageer and ambassador, I'm also contributing a little bit to modularity and to diversity.
I'm Yona and I'm part of the Albanian local community because I come from Albania.
So my name is Pravin Satputte, I'm from India.
So I'm Mike McGrath, I work for the platform engineering team as a manager.
I'm Ralph Bean and I have been coming to flock for five or six years now.
I used to work on the Fedora engineering team at Red Hat and so it was my full time job to work on Fedora and come to flock and work with the community.
So my name is Kanika and I'm from India.
I've been contributing to Fedora for two years now.
My name is Justin Flory, I've been a contributor to Fedora since November 2015 or so.
His name is Ricky Elrod, I am on the Fedora engineering team at Red Hat.
My name is Brian Xubir, I work for Red Hat as the Fedora community action and impact coordinator.
There basically there's a technology side and a people side and I think they're both very strong.
We do really try and follow the leading edge of open source technology and commitment to the open source part of that.
It's not just that it's the bleeding edge but we try to make sure we're following the leading edge of it and exciting stuff but also getting it to people in a useful way.
I think that's appealing, it's kind of fun stuff to work on at the operating system level so that's neat.

But also this is a really amazing group of people and we've got thousands of people who contribute every year to 3000 people to some level and a core group of Phenomab4500 people who are working every week on the project.
And they're really great generous people who have a real passion for the things we're working on so I think that's pretty appealing too.
I happily install most of the any of the nonviolent games in the Fedora repository are on our systems and I'm like how about it?
The major part of Fedora is what I love about it is it's a bleeding edge so I get the latest and the greatest of whatever that I want.
So be it building bleeding edge stuff on IoT or big data. I have whatever tools that I require to make sure my project is open running.
One of the things that I think is critical about Fedora that we are doing a better and better job messaging on is the Fedora community is way more than the production of the operating system.
There's a lot of things to do and you can get involved in them. There isn't like territorialism like you can't contribute to this component only we contribute to this component.
I think Fedora values the contributor.

The thing that I think is really important about Fedora is we provide a facility for people to do what they want to do and they can get a lot of support from their fellow community members because we bring the right kinds of people together.

I think the amazing thing for me is not just how many old faces I still see that are here but how many new faces I see and how important it is to the community to get people involved and get out of their way.
I think there's not just the common sense of shared purpose towards building Fedora the operating system and the distribution and making sure that our users are happy.
But there's this shared understanding that we're all people, we're all flawed, we all have something to bring to the table.
So let's come and talk and figure out what needs to happen, what we can do and everybody sees everybody else has important.
I think it's a very unique experience. Everybody's kind of at the same level here.
It's great.
The community by far.
The people are the people I work with are some of the smartest people I know. They're very resourceful, they're nice. I just can't say enough about it. I just love the community. It's like a family.
Fedora, I will say like anyone who is coming to the Fedora so he will not feel that there is not for him anything.
So for everyone there is something in Fedora.

It's passionate but very friendly. You see that especially at Flock, I mean it's a really tight-knit group of people that like working together and love working on what they work on. And it's a fun place to be.
I could easily see how passionate people were. Not just about the work that they were doing but also about supporting each other as like empowering and inclusive community to build better society.
It's an opportunity to build better software together.
Let's say the community is one of the main reasons why I am still part of it. Because they are really friendly. They are really friendly to the newcomers especially.
So you feel really welcome at the community. Because you know when you go to a new community and you want to be part of it.
First of all you are free that someone might say okay but you don't know this question but not at all. They will be really friendly with you. They will support you for everything that you might need.
And they will show you even the right direction where to go and which teams you can be in part.
The community of people who kind of use open sources and excuse to change the world. Which that's an easy thing to say. But we do it a lot through non-code contributions.

We have a huge outreach program. We have huge marketing opportunities, writing opportunities. There's ways for people to become involved in the ideals of open source even if they choose not to actually commit a line of what we as engineers would call source.

youtube_description:
Meet members of the Fedora Project community from the annual Fedora contributor conference, Flock in 2017!

What did they have to say when we asked them about Fedora? Hear what they had to say in interviews conducted at Flock 2017.

Special thanks to Chhavi Shrivastava for compiling and editing the video. Thanks also goes to Casey Stegman, Dan Courcy, and Rohit Lakshman for collecting the video and conducting interviews at Flock.
